content:
According to Mark Gurman's latest Power On newsletter, Apple is reportedly considering revamping its App Store, with the goal of boosting the platform's potential revenue.

Apple's specific plans for the App Store remain unclear. Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman reports that Apple wants to "find ways to improve profit margins and generate more recurring revenue from it," a direction being driven primarily by incoming CEO John Ternus and current Senior Vice President of Services Eddy Cue.

Reportedly, this work is one of the reasons veteran Phil Schiller left Apple last week. Schiller stepped down as Senior Vice President of Marketing back in 2020 and took on the role of Apple Fellow, with part of his responsibilities including overseeing the App Store. Schiller disagreed with this idea:

Apple has many ways it could improve App Store margins. It could eliminate the manual app review process—in the era of agentic coding, this costly procedure is no longer as effective as it once was. However, users may not welcome further automation of reviews, even if it helps reduce costs.

Apple could raise the developer membership fee, which currently stands at USD 99 per year. Given that many small developers already spend USD 200 a month on Codex and Claude subscriptions to build apps, some might argue that Apple has room to raise prices and developers would still pay. Apple could also charge large developers monthly fees based on usage, passing on some of the infrastructure costs to them.

The ultimate outcome remains to be seen, but I'm personally looking forward to seeing what form these changes ultimately take.
